title: The Original X-Men - Nautilus
gist: Teaser of a history piece arguing that British universities' shift from pure teaching to original research — symbolized by Cambridge's October 1926 adoption of sabbaticals — was driven by a Victorian scientific group called the X Club. Text is truncated before the X Club story itself.

insights.claim: Cambridge University amended its statutes in October 1926 to give academics the right to take every seventh term off, institutionalizing the sabbatical.
insights.speaker: Thomas W. Hodgkinson
insights.so_what: Institutional rules that protect research time are long-lived structural drivers of a nation's scientific output.
insights.quote: It introduced the right for academics to take every seventh term off.

insights.claim: In academia a sabbatical is not rest but a reallocation from teaching to original research, signaling that universities valued scholarship beyond instruction.
insights.speaker: Thomas W. Hodgkinson
insights.so_what: Watch how universities budget teaching vs. research time amid funding pressure; it shapes the pipeline of basic research.
insights.quote: Yet in an academic context, it usually means a rest from one kind of work, so that you can focus on another.

insights.claim: The transformation of universities' core purpose toward independent research was driven by a group of British scientists who called themselves the X Club.
insights.speaker: Thomas W. Hodgkinson
insights.so_what: Small, coordinated elite networks can reshape institutions over decades — a pattern relevant to how science policy gets made.
insights.quote: a transformation that was driven by a mysterious-sounding group of British scientists who called themselves the “X Club.”
